title: Cop fired shots after seeing gun
subtitle: 'I'll never forget that sound ... I realized, oh my God, it's a toy'
article: A soft-spoken Vancouver police officer described Monday the split- second decisions he had to make before shooting a suspected car thief who reached for the brown handle of what looked like a gun.

Constable Darren Foster told a coroner's inquest he discovered the gun was a plastic replica only after he fired three bullets at Thomas Evon Stevenson, the 46-year-old cocaine user who died in a stolen car on Dec. 7, 2002.
When the shooting stopped, Stevenson was slumped over in the front seat of the Toyota Camry, with bullet wounds in his abdomen, his chest and the aorta of his heart, as well as wounds on both hands.
Another police officer reached through a shattered window of the car, grabbed the gun, and threw it on the pavement.
"I'll never forget that sound," said Foster, his voice straining with emotion. "That plastic sound of a child's toy on the pavement. I realized, oh my God, it's a toy."
That was some of the dramatic testimony on the first day of a public inquest in Burnaby into a shooting that took place in the 400- block East Pender.

Foster, a 12-year-veteran of the Vancouver police department, said he frequently checked East Pender for stolen vehicles, because he said criminals often left cars there, and often used stolen vehicles to commit other crimes.

That December evening more than two years ago, Foster noticed a white Toyota Camry he didn't recognize. He used the laptop computer in his marked police vehicle to run a licence plate check and immediately discovered the vehicle was stolen.

Foster left his police cruiser and touched the front hood of the Camry. The hood was still warm, which indicated to Foster the vehicle was recently used. He radioed in his plan to watch the vehicle to see if someone would return to it, and asked other officers to back him up.

Foster popped open the hood, pulled a few spark plug wires and disconnected a starter wire to make sure the car couldn't start. The door was unlocked, so he went inside, noted the ignition had been stripped off, and stuck a knife in the ignition to ensure the car still couldn't start.

Then Foster parked his police cruiser in an alley and hid behind shrubs, about 20 metres to the rear of the stolen car. He watched one man stop on the sidewalk near the car and look in all directions. Foster assumed it was a "heat check" -- a criminal's check for the "heat," or police, before committing a crime. But the first man continued to the corner and started looking around again, and Foster didn't immediately notice a second man --Stevenson -- until he was behind the car. Stevenson opened the driver's door and hopped in.

Foster said he advised the nearest backup officer -- Sergeant Clive Milligan -- that someone had gone into the vehicle. Another backup officer -- one with a police dog -- reported that he was too far away to help.
Foster said he then jogged up to the car and stopped behind the driver's door. He arrived with his semi-automatic pistol already drawn.
Foster said he shouted out: "Vancouver police! Show me your hands!"

He said Stevenson appeared to be startled and looked to the rear, over his shoulder, as he put up both hands. Foster said the suspect kept both hands up "for a brief millisecond" before reaching over to the driver's door and locking it.
Stevenson then leaned forwards. Foster thought it was a futile attempt to start the car but he was worried, because he couldn't see Stevenson's hands, and didn't know what he was doing.
Foster said he continued to order Stevenson to "show me your hands" and "unlock the door," but Stevenson didn't obey instructions.
Instead, as the officer watched, Stevenson used a lighter to light a crack cocaine pipe.

Stevenson said he reported by radio that he had a male suspect at gunpoint who was refusing to get out of his vehicle. Milligan arrived in his police cruiser five to 10 seconds later, parked nose- to-nose with the stolen Toyota, and shone an intensely bright "take down light" into the vehicle.
Foster said he still couldn't see what Stevenson was doing, even when Stevenson was using the lighter, because the window was fogged.
"I felt the dialogue was over and I needed to extricate him," he told coroner Nicholas Snyckers and the three-woman, two-man coroner's jury.

Foster struck the driver's side window three times, and it didn't break until the third strike. Foster said Stevenson was inching away from the driver's window, toward the passenger window, when the driver's window shattered.
Then Milligan shouted out: "He's got a gun! He's got a gun in his jacket"

Foster said Stevenson had his shoulders partly turned away from him but, "for a split second," he saw what appeared to be the brown wooden handle of some kind of semi-automatic gun in Stevenson's jacket.
"I remember a flash and a pop," Foster said. "I didn't know where it was coming. I didn't know if I was being shot at."
Foster told the inquest he remembered firing two shots, but later learned from police reports that he had fired three.
The inquest is scheduled to continue to Friday.

Forensic pathologist Dr. Charles Lee told the inquest there could have been as many as six shots and as few as three shots, but gunshot wounds to the chest and abdomen area were the cause of death -- particularly the bullets that hit the lung, the heart and aorta.

Dr. Graham James, a forensic toxicologist who checked body samples for drugs and alcohol, said he found concentrations of methadone that would have killed someone who had not developed a tolerance to the heroin substitute. He also found a high concentration of cocaine in Stevenson's blood. James concluded that Stevenson had either used a large amount of cocaine just before his death, or had been on a coke binge during the hours or days before his death.
